new_statements.rule_in_words: In Marind, including the Bian (Mbian) language, primary stress falls on the last syllable of the root (not necessarily of the inflected/compounded word); in Bian Marind the unstressed pretonic vowels were lost (kmaɣ, mhuk, bhik, iz'mi, af'si, wah'ni), and a paragogic e/a added after a closed final syllable is unstressed, so surface stress stays on the root-final syllable. This is Usher's comparative reading of Drabbe's stress-marked Boven-Mbian data plus Drabbe's 1955 rule for coastal Marind; no first-hand Bian-specific rule statement was opened.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Usher: trisyllabic roots carried secondary stress on the initial syllable (the medial syllable then syncopated in Mbian). Geurtjens 1926:3-4 (coastal): alternating secondary stress when more than two syllables precede the main stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Usher (after Drabbe 1955:16): compounds and inflected forms need not be final-stressed; stress 'sometimes contrastive due to inflection and compounding'. Geurtjens 1933:385: added final e/a in Boven-Biansch is unstressed (breve-marked in his list). Coastal parallels (Geurtjens 1926:3-5; Olsson 2017 sec. 2.3): penult stress in proper names, suffixed derivations, schwa-final words.
new_statements.domain_note: Root (stem) domain per Usher/Drabbe; Drabbe 1954 forms are citation forms of roots from Kolam village. Inflected verbs (prefixal complex) not covered for Bian Marind.
new_statements.identity_note: Usher's 'Mbian' / Drabbe's 'Boven-Mbian' (Kolam village) and Geurtjens' 'Boven-Biansch' are the same variety as Glottolog bian1251 Bian Marind (bpv), upper Bian River, Muting district. The explicit stress rules opened first-hand (Geurtjens 1926:3-5; Olsson 2017 sec. 2.3) describe Coastal Marind (nucl1622: Gawir/Eastern and Western dialects), a separate language; Usher's root-final statement is made for the Marind group as a whole and applied to Mbian through its syncope pattern.

sources.note: Second-hand (after Drabbe 1955:16 and Drabbe 1954 data): stress falls on the final syllable of the root (realised as a pitch rise); trisyllabic roots get secondary stress on the initial syllable, which 'led to syncope and the formation of medial consonant clusters in Mbian and Kumb'; Mbian (=Bian Marind) forms are cited with Drabbe-1954 stress marks, all final: iz'mi 'sago petiole', af'si 'tears', wah'ni 'body', hi'kam 'accompany', sasa'hi 'work', wa'ninggap 'good'; stress 'sometimes contrastive due to inflection and compounding (Drabbe 1955:16)'.

sources.note: First-hand on Boven-Biansch but no stress-position rule: p.385 'Vele woorden, vooral zij die op een gesloten lettergreep eindigen, krijgen als toeslag een onbetoonde e of a' (many words, especially those ending in a closed syllable, take an added UNSTRESSED e or a); the list marks this vowel with a breve (abligĕ, afsarĕ, aghiĕ). Otherwise only segmental differences from the coast language (gh, r, a~e).

sources.note: No stress statement for Bian Marind. Says the only Bian Marind descriptions are Drabbe 1954 (short description of the verb) and Drabbe's ms. wordlist plus SIL unpublished wordlists; Olsson worked two weeks in Muting (2016). Notes Bian Marind 'permit[s] consonant clusters that are impossible in Coastal Marind, e.g. [kmaɣ] inside (Coastal kumaɣ), [mhuk] Crowned Pigeon (Coastal mahuk), [bhik] pig (Coastal basik)' -- i.e. loss of the pretonic vowel. Coastal Marind: stress root-final, marked by higher pitch, weight-insensitive, penult in (historically) suffixed forms.
